page: Microsoft Azure E96-48as_v4 is a memory-optimized virtual machine belonging to the EASv4 server family, running on the Microsoft Hyper-V hypervisor. It is equipped with an AMD EPYC 7763 processor featuring 24 physical cores and 48 vCPUs with dedicated allocation, operating at a clock speed of 3.525 GHz. The system includes 672.0 GB of RAM, yielding a high memory-to-core ratio of 14.0 GB per core. Local storage consists of a 1376 GB SSD, and the instance is Premium Storage capable. No GPU accelerators are present.

In benchmark evaluations, the server demonstrates strong multi-core and single-core CPU performance, as evidenced by its stress-ng scores and a PassMark CPU score of 51926.65. Multi-threaded bzip3 decompression and Geekbench multi-core performance also rank in the top 25%. However, memory bandwidth for large block read and write operations remains in the average tier, alongside standard database operations and Redis SET throughput. While the system handles small-model LLM inference efficiently, text generation for large 70B models is a notable bottleneck, registering in the bottom 10% of benchmarks.

The high memory density relative to the vCPU count makes this instance a resource-efficient option for workloads requiring large memory footprints without the overhead of additional compute cores. It supports memory-intensive applications such as large-scale databases, in-memory caching, data analytics, and memory-bound enterprise applications.
description: Microsoft Azure E96-48as_v4 is an x86_64 memory-optimized virtual machine from the EASv4 family, powered by an AMD EPYC 7763 processor. It features 48 dedicated vCPUs (24 physical cores) running at 3.525 GHz, 672.0 GB of RAM, and a 1376 GB local SSD. The server delivers strong multi-core CPU performance, ranking in the top 25% for stress-ng and PassMark CPU benchmarks, though memory bandwidth and database operations perform in the average tier. With a high memory-to-core ratio of 14.0 GB per core, this instance provides qualitative cost efficiency for memory-heavy workloads by minimizing unnecessary compute overhead. It supports large-scale databases, in-memory caching, and data processing tasks, though its lack of GPU acceleration and poor large-model LLM text generation speeds limit its utility for heavy AI training workloads.
